course.name: Templates, Packages & the Store
course.description: Don't build from scratch — install, evaluate, fork, template, and publish.
course.longDescription: Your team keeps rebuilding the same three flows for every new client. This course ends that: shop the store and the package registry before you build, read permissions and ratings like a skeptic, freeze proven flows into versioned templates, share apps without losing control of visibility and forks, and finally publish one app through store review. By the end you own a shared template library — and a listing with your name on it.

modules.title: Don't Rebuild It
modules.description: Shop the store and the package registry — and judge what you find before you trust it.

lessons.title: Why Build What Someone Already Built?

challenges.prompt: Priya wants to see what community apps and packages already exist before rebuilding the triage flow. Where does she look?
challenges.explanation: The Explore hub carries both shelves — community apps and the package registry (Packages in its header) — and the home screen previews it with Featured and Top Charts. Developer Tools is the tempting miss: it's where you BUILD packages, not where you discover them.

options.label: The Explore hub in the sidebar — community apps plus the Packages registry
Developer Tools — that's where packages live
Any board's node menu — it lists everything installable
Settings — reuse is configured per device

challenges.prompt: You installed a mail package from the registry, but its nodes don't appear in the client app's catalog. What's the most likely cause?
challenges.explanation: Installing puts code on the device; only linking (Add Package in the app's own Packages screen) declares the dependency that fills that app's catalog. Reinstalling Flow-Like is the classic wasted afternoon — the device copy was never the problem. Verification status affects trust signals, not whether linked nodes load.

options.label: The package is installed on the device but never linked to this app
The Flow-Like installation is corrupted — reinstall it
Unverified packages can't expose nodes until review completes
The app must be published before third-party nodes activate

challenges.prompt: Which statements about the three package scopes are true?
challenges.explanation: Registry, device, and app are deliberately separate: discover in Explore → Packages, manage the device copy in Library → Packages, and declare per-app versions in each app's Packages screen. The tempting wrong pick is the auto-update one — updating the device copy never rewrites an app's linked version, which is exactly why old client apps keep working after a device update.

options.label: The registry in Explore → Packages is where you discover package versions
Library → Packages manages what's installed on this computer
Linking records the package version an app requires, filling its catalog
Updating the device copy automatically updates every app's linked version
Uninstalling from the device also removes the dependency from each app

challenges.prompt: A package card carries the verification shield. What does that actually tell you?
challenges.explanation: The shield records that the package completed the registry's review process — a review state, nothing more. The tempting read is "safe to install without checking": verification is explicitly not a security warranty and says nothing about future versions, so you still review permissions, author, and source links yourself.

options.label: It completed the registry's verification process — a review state, not a warranty
It's safe to install without reviewing its permissions
It was built by the Flow-Like team
It requests no permissions at all

challenges.prompt: "Inbox Wizard" declares HTTP access to any host plus user-scoped storage. Which moves belong in your evaluation?
challenges.explanation: The rule is: compare the declaration with what the nodes are supposed to do — which means opening Permissions AND Nodes, then weighing author, source links, and reviews. "Verified means the declaration was already judged harmless" is the tempting skip: verification records review state and doesn't pre-answer whether THESE capabilities fit YOUR client app.

options.label: Ask whether any-host network access is coherent for what these nodes claim to do
Open the Nodes tab to see what the package actually exports
Weigh the author, source links, and user reviews on the detail page
Skip the check — the verified badge means the permissions were already cleared as harmless
Evaluate once and assume future versions keep identical behavior

challenges.prompt: You fork a public support app to evaluate it. It opens with flows and widgets — but no storage files. Why?
challenges.explanation: The owner defines the fork policy; the fork dialog only displays what you'll receive, and this owner chose not to ship files. "Files sync in later" is the tempting one — a fork is a one-time copy with no ongoing link to the source, so nothing arrives afterwards in either direction.

options.label: The owner's fork policy excludes files — the dialog showed exactly this result
Storage syncs into the fork over the next hours
It's a bug — forks copy everything by definition
You unticked files in the fork dialog — the person forking picks the contents

modules.title: Share and Ship
modules.description: Freeze proven flows into templates, share the app on your terms, and publish it through store review.

challenges.prompt: You create a template from the triage flow and pick "Latest" as the source. What does the template capture?
challenges.explanation: Latest means "the draft as it is right now" — the template freezes that state at creation and stops. The tempting answer is the subscription: templates never keep following later draft edits; that's the exact misconception that produces stale June templates in July.

options.label: The current draft, frozen at the moment of creation
A live link — the template keeps following future draft edits
The newest numbered version, not the draft
Nothing yet — templates only fill once the app is published

challenges.prompt: Priya templated "Customer Support Automation" last month, then kept improving the draft. Apps created from the template today lack every improvement. What's the fix?
challenges.explanation: A template is a snapshot shelf: import the improved flow as another template version, and older versions stay for consumers who want them. Re-saving the draft changes nothing the template can see, and the app's Version field is human-facing release metadata — editing it snapshots nothing.

options.label: Import the improved flow snapshot as a new template version
Re-save the draft — the template refreshes on save
Bump the app's Version field so the template updates
Delete and recreate the app from scratch

challenges.prompt: Which of these travel inside a Flow Template?
challenges.explanation: A template carries the captured flow graph plus its own name, description, and versions — that's the whole cargo. Runtime variables, events, and storage staying behind is the point, not a gap: a template shares one reusable graph, while sharing a full project is what apps (and forks) are for.

options.label: The captured flow graph
The template's own name, description, and versions
The source app's runtime variables and credentials
The source app's events
The source app's storage files

challenges.prompt: Your app is Private and the neighboring team wants in. What's the minimum visibility that lets you invite them?
challenges.explanation: Private means synced for your account only — no Team page, no invites. Prototype is the sharing threshold: Team appears in the navigation and you can invite collaborators. The public rungs would work too, but they're store levels that go through review — far more than an internal invite needs.

options.label: Prototype — invites unlock there
Private — invites work at every online level
Public Request — someone must be able to request access first
Public — sharing means the store

challenges.prompt: Which statements about the fork policy are true?
challenges.explanation: The owner sets the policy, the databases choice is genuinely three-way, and every fork gets its own Owner, Admin, and User roles no matter what — that floor can't be turned off. The tempting wrong pick is the forker choosing: the fork dialog only displays the owner's decision, it never offers checkboxes to the person forking.

options.label: The app's owner defines the policy; the fork dialog only shows the result
Databases can ship as tables with data, tables only, or not at all
A fork always gets its own Owner, Admin, and User roles, even when custom roles don't travel
The person forking ticks which pieces they want to take
A fork keeps a live link, so the owner's future edits flow in

challenges.prompt: The app is Prototype with four collaborators, and you switch it to Private. What happens?
challenges.explanation: Private means your account only, so the downgrade removes all collaborators and they lose access immediately — the switch warns you for exactly this reason. Review only guards the public rungs, and a Prototype app was never store-listed, so there's nothing to delist.

options.label: All four collaborators are removed and lose access immediately
Existing members stay; only new invites are blocked
Nothing yet — the downgrade waits for central review
The app is removed from its store listing

challenges.prompt: Friday, 16:50: Priya flips the app from Prototype to Public. Is it in the store on Monday morning?
challenges.explanation: Public transitions submit the app for central review, which takes one to three business days — flipped on Friday evening, Monday is optimistic. "Instantly listed" is the tempting answer the review gate exists to prevent; and nothing about submission removes your collaborators.

options.label: Probably not — the switch submits it for central review, which takes 1–3 business days
Yes — Public takes effect the moment it's saved
Only after her collaborators are removed, which the switch does first
Only if she bumps the app's Version field before flipping

challenges.prompt: Before submitting, Priya sets the app's Version field to "2.0". What did that actually do?
challenges.explanation: The app Version field is free-form release metadata for people browsing — a label for a tested collection of flow and interface versions. It snapshots nothing: flow versions are created per-board in Manage Board, and events keep whatever target they had. Mixing the two up is how "versioned" apps still serve drafts.

options.label: Changed a human-facing release label — no snapshot of flows, storage, or events
Froze an immutable snapshot of the entire app
Created version 2.0 of every flow in the app
Pinned all events to their current flow versions

challenges.prompt: Which steps belong in the pre-publication pass for the support kit?
challenges.explanation: A listing needs honest metadata, store-facing events pinned to numbered versions so draft edits never reach strangers, and a deliberate fork policy for what public forkers may take. The tempting extra is the detour rung: Prototype can move straight to Public — routing through Public Request first is a choice, not a requirement.

options.label: Write a name and description that tell store visitors what the app does
Pin production-facing events to numbered flow versions instead of Latest
Re-decide the fork policy — what should a stranger's fork contain?
Switch to Public Request first — Prototype can't reach Public directly
Set the app Version field so the release is frozen against edits

modules.title: Final Assessment
modules.description: One week, four asks, four findings — run the template library like you own it.

challenges.prompt: Finding F1: the new teammate installed the mail package from Explore → Packages, but its nodes are missing from the client app's catalog. What closes F1?
challenges.explanation: Install and linkage are separate scopes: the device has the code, but the client app never declared the dependency. Add Package in that app's Packages screen, then reload the flow. Reinstalling attacks the scope that was already fine, and verification state never gates whether a linked package's nodes load.

options.label: Link the package in the client app's Packages screen, then reload the flow
Uninstall and reinstall the package on the laptop
Wait for the package's verification review to finish
Publish the client app — store review activates third-party nodes

challenges.prompt: Ask 3: the partner org evaluates by forking, and client rows must never leave the app. Which fork-policy decisions are right?
challenges.explanation: "Tables only" ships structure without a single client row — exactly compliance's line — and keeping flows and templates on is what makes the evaluation worth anything. The trap options break the model: turning roles off can't strip the Owner/Admin/User floor every fork receives, and a fork has no live link back, so "revoke later" revokes nothing already copied.

options.label: Set databases to tables only, so structure arrives but client rows don't
Keep flows and templates enabled so the blueprint is actually evaluable
Toggle roles off so the fork arrives without any Owner or Admin role
Ship full data — you can revoke the fork's copy remotely after the evaluation
Ask the partner to untick databases themselves in the fork dialog

challenges.prompt: Finding F4: apps created from the June template still show the June routing bug, even though the draft was fixed and versioned to 2.1.0 in July. What's the correct move?
challenges.explanation: The June template froze the draft at creation — "Latest" is a moment, not a subscription — so the July fix never entered it. Import the 2.1.0 snapshot as a new template version; the June version stays available for deliberate choice. Re-saving the draft or relabeling the app changes nothing a template consumer receives.

options.label: Import the fixed 2.1.0 snapshot as a new version of the template
Re-save the triage draft so the June template picks up the fix
Bump the app's Version field to signal the template is current
Delete the template — templates can't be updated once created

challenges.prompt: Ask 4: Friday's demo needs the partner to find the store listing and request access. It's Monday and the app is Prototype. What's the plan?
challenges.explanation: "Request to join" is Public Request, and reaching any public rung goes through central review — one to three business days — so the switch must happen today, not Thursday night. Full Public would let everyone join directly, and Prototype is never store-listed no matter how many invite links you mint.

options.label: Switch to Public Request today — review can take 1–3 business days
Flip it Thursday evening; visibility changes apply instantly
Go full Public — requesting access is the default everywhere
Stay Prototype and send an invite link — that's what store visitors use

challenges.prompt: Ask 2: the neighboring team wants the triage graph only — no storage, events, or roles. What do you hand them?
challenges.explanation: One reusable graph is precisely a Flow Template's cargo: the versioned snapshot travels, and variables, events, storage, and roles all stay behind by design. Inviting them into the app or waiting for the store listing shares a whole project boundary — everything they said they didn't want.

options.label: A Flow Template of the triage flow's proven version
An invite — membership in the Customer Support Copilot app
The store listing, once review completes
A full fork with databases set to tables and data

challenges.prompt: Findings F2 (a device package update broke an older client app) and F3 (a store visitor saw last night's half-finished draft). Which responses actually close them?
challenges.explanation: F2 is the scope split: each app keeps its own linked version, so device updates get reviewed per app before they're assumed safe. F3 is the pinning rule: store-facing events target numbered versions so drafts stay invisible, and the changelog plus Version label make the eventual update legible. The trap answers re-open the findings — device updates never rewrite app declarations, and dropping to Private "just for a moment" evicts every collaborator immediately.

options.label: Review each app's Packages screen before applying device-wide updates
Pin store-facing events to numbered flow versions so drafts never reach visitors
Ship the reviewed fix as a new flow version, then update the changelog and Version label
Treat the device update as complete — apps follow the device copy automatically
Drop the app to Private while cleaning up the draft; collaborators keep access meanwhile
